Real-rootedness of rook-Eulerian polynomials

Per Alexandersson Address: Department of Mathematics, Stockholm University, SE-106 91 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: per.w.alexandersson@gmail.com , Aryaman Jal Address: Department of Mathematics, KTH Royal Institute of Technology SE-100 44 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: aryaman@kth.se and Maena Quemener Address: Department of Mathematics, École normale supérieure Paris-Saclay 4, avenue des Sciences 91190, Gif-sur-Yvette Email address: maena.quemener@ens-paris-saclay.fr
Abstract.

We introduce rook-Eulerian polynomials, a generalization of the classical Eulerian polynomials arising from complete rook placements on Ferrers boards, and prove that they are real-rooted. We show that a natural context in which to interpret these rook placements is as lower intervals of 312312-avoiding permutations in the Bruhat order. We end with some variations and generalizations along this theme.

Key words and phrases:
Ferrers board, rook placements, Bruhat order, real-rootedness
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A15, 05A15, 26C10

In this note, we study rook-Eulerian polynomials, a generalization of the classical Eulerian polynomials, which arise from complete rook placements on Ferrers boards. Using the framework of sequences of interlacing polynomials, we prove that rook-Eulerian polynomials are real-rooted. We then revisit a folklore fact: complete rook placements on Ferrers boards have a natural poset structure, namely the lower order ideal of a 312312-avoiding permutation in the Bruhat order. The 312312-avoiding nature of the permutation is necessary for the real-rootedness to hold. We contrast rook-Eulerian polynomials with 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomials, and show that the two families overlap without coinciding with one another. Finally we consider descent-generating polynomials of lower intervals in the weak order on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} and show that while they are not real-rooted in general, are likely to have ultra-log-concave coefficients.

1. Preliminaries

A board BB is a subset of the square grid [n]×[n][n]\times[n]. By a non-attacking placement of rooks on a board, we mean a subset S⊂BS\subset B such that no two elements of SS share the same xx-coordinate or yy-coordinate. This corresponds to a placement of rooks on BB such that no two rooks can take each other in the sense of chess. Hereafter, the boards in question will arise from partitions λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) with λ1≤λ2≤…≤λn\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots\leq\lambda_{n}. We will use the words partition and Ferrers board interchangeably. We use the French convention for drawing Ferrers boards: left-justified arrays of boxes are drawn such that the first has λ1\lambda_{1} cells, the second below it has λ2\lambda_{2} cells and so on. The columns of the board are labeled from 11 to nn from left to right.

Definition 1.

A complete rook placement on a Ferrers board is a rook placement such that each column and row contains exactly one rook.

We note that in order to have at least one complete rook placement, λ\lambda must satisfy λi≥i\lambda_{i}\geq i for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. It will be useful to view complete rook placements as permutations. To that end, given a complete rook placement on a shape λ\lambda with nn parts, define a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, with σi\sigma_{i} equal to the index of the column of the rook placed in the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} row. See Figure 1 for an example.

The full permutation group carries two natural and extensively studied poset structures that we recall below.

Definition 2 (Weak and strong order).

The weak order on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} is a partial order, where the cover relations are defined as follows. The permutation π\pi covers σ\sigma if σ\sigma can be obtained from π\pi by an adjacent transposition that decreases the number of inversions. An adjacent transposition refers to a swap of adjacent elements in σ\sigma. We write σ≤Wπ\sigma\leq_{W}\pi if σ\sigma is less than or equal to π\pi in the weak order.

Similarly, the strong order or Bruhat order is defined in the same manner, but here the transposition need not be adjacent. We denote this relation by σ≤Bπ\sigma\leq_{B}\pi.

The maximal element in both orders is unique, and given by the longest permutation ω0=[n,…,2,1]\omega_{0}=[n,\dotsc,2,1].

Recall that a permutation σ\sigma contains the pattern 312312 if there exists i<j<ki<j<k such that σj<σk<σi\sigma_{j}<\sigma_{k}<\sigma_{i}. If this does not hold, we say that σ\sigma is 312312-avoiding.

The following proposition is a folklore fact in Catalan combinatorics; we include a proof for completeness. Rows and columns of BB are indexed by coordinates (i,j)∈[n]×[n](i,j)\in[n]\times[n]. A pair of rooks (i,j)(i,j) and (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) is non-nested if i<ki<k and ℓ<j\ell<j, and nested otherwise. In terms of rooks on the board, non-nesting means means that one rook does not occur South-East of another. Given a pair of non-nested rooks (i,j)(i,j) and (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) define the switch move11 1 Develin uses the same terminology but with λ\lambda drawn according to the English convention [Dev06]. on rook (i,j)(i,j) to be the swap that replaces the given pair of rooks with (k,j)(k,j) and (i,ℓ)(i,\ell). Similarly, define the inverse switch move to be the swap that replaces a pair of nested rooks with their non-nesting counterpart.

Proposition 3.

Every 312312-avoiding permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} corresponds to a Ferrers board λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{n}) with λi≥i\lambda_{i}\geq i for i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1 and λn=n\lambda_{n}=n, and vice-versa. The permutations in the interval

{π∈𝔖n:id≤Bπ≤Bσ}\{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}:\mathrm{id}\leq_{B}\pi\leq_{B}\sigma\}

are exactly the complete rook placements on the Ferrers board λ\lambda.

Proof.

For n≥1n\geq 1, let 𝔖312\mathfrak{S}_{312} and Λ\Lambda respectively be the set of 312312-avoiding permutations on [n][n], and the Ferrers diagrams λ\lambda fitting inside an [n]×[n][n]\times[n] grid satisfying λi≥i\lambda_{i}\geq i. We define a bijection from 𝔖312\mathfrak{S}_{312} to Λ\Lambda as follows. Given σ∈𝔖312\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{312} define a complete rook placement ρ\rho on [n]×[n][n]\times[n] by

ρ={(i,σi):i∈[n]}\rho=\{(i,\sigma_{i}):i\in[n]\}

and let λ\lambda be the Ferrers boards defined such that the last cell of every row of λ\lambda either contains a rook of ρ\rho or has a rook of ρ\rho above it in the same column. The fact that σ\sigma is a permutation immediately implies that λi≥i\lambda_{i}\geq i. Further, every such λ\lambda arises from a complete rook placement: given λ\lambda, define ρ′\rho^{\prime} by placing a rook in (1,λ1)(1,\lambda_{1}) and for i∈[2,n]i\in[2,n] place a rook as far to the right as possible such that it does not attack the rooks that have already been placed in rows 11 to i−1i-1. This is clearly a complete rook placement on λ\lambda; let σ′\sigma^{\prime} be the permutation corresponding to ρ′\rho^{\prime}.

Claim: The permutation σ\sigma avoids 312312.

To see this, note that the presence of a 312312 pattern in σ′\sigma^{\prime} corresponds to three rooks in ρ′\rho^{\prime} in a configuration as in Figure 2 (after deleting the rows and columns not involved in the 312312 pattern). This is a contradiction since by construction, the rooks in each row of ρ′\rho^{\prime} are placed as far to the right as possible without attacking the rooks above that row.

For the second claim, fix σ∈𝔖312\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{312} and let ℛλ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda} be the set of complete rook placements on λ\lambda, where ρmax\rho_{\max} is the rook placement corresponding to σ\sigma. Let f:[id,σ]B→ℛλf:[\mathrm{id},\sigma]_{B}\to\mathcal{R}_{\lambda} be the map that associates a permutation π\pi with its complete rook placement ρπ\rho_{\pi} on [n]×[n][n]\times[n]. We need to show that ρπ\rho_{\pi} lies on λ\lambda. Since π≤Bσ\pi\leq_{B}\sigma, π\pi can be obtained from σ\sigma by a series of transpositions. For every such transposition (i,j)(i,j), perform the corresponding switch move to the rooks in rows ii and jj in the rook placement. The resulting rook placement is ρπ\rho_{\pi}. This shows that ρπ\rho_{\pi} lies in ℛλ\mathcal{R}_{\lambda}. In the opposite direction, given a rook placement ρ\rho on λ\lambda, let the corresponding permutation be π\pi. We need to show that π≤Bσ\pi\leq_{B}\sigma. We will first show that we can obtain ρmax\rho_{\max} from ρ\rho as follows: for every row ii from 11 to nn, if ρ\rho has no rook in (i,σi)(i,\sigma_{i}), perform the inverse switch the nested rooks (i,πi)(i,\pi_{i}) and (j,σi)(j,\sigma_{i}) where j>ij>i is the row index containing a rook of ρ\rho in column σi\sigma_{i}. (This pair of rooks is indeed nested because πi<σi\pi_{i}<\sigma_{i}, which holds since the rook of ρmax\rho_{\max} in row ii is placed as far to the right as possible.) The rook placement obtained after this procedure is clearly ρmax\rho_{\max}. By performing the same sequence of transpositions corresponding to the inverse switch moves, we can obtain σ\sigma from π\pi, which shows that π≤Bσ\pi\leq_{B}\sigma. See Figure 3 for an example of this correspondence. ∎

One can show that the correspondence in the second half of the theorem holds more generally for complete rook placements on skew shapes, see [Sjö07, Proposition 12] for instance.

Definition 5.

An ascent in a complete rook placement σ\sigma is an index i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that σi<σi+1\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{i+1}. In other words, the rook in row i+1i+1 lies strictly to the right of the rook in row ii. We also extend the notion of ascents to words, i.e., if w1​w2​…​wℓw_{1}w_{2}\dotsc w_{\ell} is a word, then ii is an ascent of the word if wi<wi+1w_{i}<w_{i+1}.

Example 6.

The rook placement σ=31524687\sigma=31524687 from Example 4 has 2,4,52,4,5 and 66 as ascents.

We denote by πλ\pi_{\lambda} the 312312-avoiding permutation corresponding to λ\lambda. By Proposition 3, the set of complete rook placements on λ\lambda is the interval [id,πλ][\id,\pi_{\lambda}] in the Bruhat order. The rook-Eulerian polynomial of λ\lambda is defined as

Qλ​(t)≔∑σ∈[id,πλ]Btasc⁡(σ).{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}Q^{\lambda}(t)}\coloneqq\sum_{\sigma\in[\id,\pi_{\lambda}]_{B}}t^{\asc(\sigma)}.

When λ=(n,…,n)\lambda=(n,\dots,n), the corresponding interval is the full permutation group 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} and the associated QλQ^{\lambda} is the Eulerian polynomial An​(t)A_{n}(t), the real-rootedness of which is well-known [Fro10].

This polynomial has arisen in the context of rook theory before. For example, Qλ​(t)Q^{\lambda}(t) can be obtained as the q=1q=1 specialization of the polynomial t−1​AF​(t,q)t^{-1}A_{F}(t,q) considered in [SY12], where FF is the Ferrers board λ\lambda. The main result of [SY12] states that AF​(t,q)A_{F}(t,q) can be expressed as a permanent of a matrix the entries of which are area-generating polynomials of lattice paths. In a different context, evaluating QλQ^{\lambda} at t=1t=1 and taking the square yields the number of Hamiltonian paths in the Ferrers graph corresponding to λ\lambda [EvW04, Theorem 3.3].

2. Real-rootedness of rook-Eulerian polynomials

In this section, we prove the real-rootedness of Qλ​(t)Q^{\lambda}(t) and some generalizations of this family of polynomials. We first widen the scope of Ferrers boards under consideration.

Suppose now that λ\lambda satisfies λi≥i\lambda_{i}\geq i for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and we do not require that λn=n\lambda_{n}=n holds. A row-complete rook placement on λ\lambda is a placement of rooks such that every row contains a rook, and every column contains at most one rook. Let SλS_{\lambda} denote the set of row-complete rook placements on λ\lambda.

Similar to the previous section, a row-complete rook placement σ\sigma is described as a word with distinct entries σ1​…​σn\sigma_{1}\dotsc\sigma_{n}, where σi\sigma_{i} denotes the column index of the rook placed in the ithi^{\textnormal{th}} row. The notion of ascent generalizes to this setting. By a minor abuse of notation, we let Qλ​(t)Q^{\lambda}(t) denote the ascent-generating polynomial for row-complete rook placements on λ\lambda. We will refer to this as the rook-Eulerian polynomial on λ\lambda. As we will only talk about row-complete rook placements in this section, we will sometimes refer to these objects only as “rook placements.”

In order to prove real-rootedness of Qλ​(t)Q^{\lambda}(t), we need to introduce a refinement. Consider the set of rook placements on λ\lambda such that column index of the rook placed in the first row is ii. Its associated ascent-generating polynomial is

(1) Qiλ​(t)≔∑σ∈Sλσ1=itasc⁡(σ).{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}Q^{\lambda}_{i}(t)}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in S_{\lambda}\\ \sigma_{1}=i\end{subarray}}t^{\asc(\sigma)}.

By conditioning on the value of the first entry in the word, it is clear that these polynomials refine QλQ^{\lambda} and that we have

(2) Qλ​(t)=∑i=1λ1Qiλ​(t).Q^{\lambda}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda_{1}}Q^{\lambda}_{i}(t).

Definition 8.

Let ff and gg be polynomials with positive leading coefficients and real, non-positive zeros, aia_{i} and bib_{i}, respectively. We say that ff interlaces gg, and we write f⪯g{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f\preceq g} if

⋯≤a3≤b3≤a2≤b2≤a1≤b1≤0.\dotsm\leq a_{3}\leq b_{3}\leq a_{2}\leq b_{2}\leq a_{1}\leq b_{1}\leq 0.

Note that deg⁡(f)=deg⁡(g)\deg(f)=\deg(g) or deg⁡(f)+1=deg⁡(g)\deg(f)+1=\deg(g).

We also need the concept of interlacing sequences, which has proven useful for establishing real-rootedness results.

Definition 9.

A sequence F=(f1,…,fn)F=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}) of real-rooted polynomials is interlacing if fi⪯fjf_{i}\preceq f_{j} for 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n.

For all Ferrers boards of shape λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) and n>1n>1, the family of polynomials is (Qiλ)i=1λ1(Q^{\lambda}_{i})_{i=1}^{\lambda_{1}} is interlacing. In particular, the rook-Eulerian polynomial QλQ^{\lambda} is real-rooted.

2.1. A multivariate generalization

One multivariate version of the rook-Eulerian polynomials can be defined as follows

Qλ​(𝐱)=∑σ∈Sλ∏i∈Asc⁡(σ)xi,Q^{\lambda}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{\lambda}}\prod_{i\in\Asc(\sigma)}x_{i},

where Asc⁡(σ)={i∈[n−1]:σi<σi+1}\Asc(\sigma)=\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{i+1}\} and 𝐱=(x1,…,xn−1)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}).

Recall that a multivariate polynomial P⁡(x1,…,xn)P(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n}) is same-phase stable if for all μ∈ℝ+n\mathbf{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}, the univariate polynomial P⁡(t​μ)P(t\mathbf{\mu}) is real-rooted. By an identical argument as in the proof of Proposition 12, we have the following.

Theorem 13.

For all Ferrers boards λ\lambda, Qλ​(𝐱)Q^{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}) is same-phase stable.

In the case of λ=(n)n\lambda=(n)^{n}, same-phase stability was proved earlier in [AN21], where it was also observed that stability of Qλ​(𝐱)Q^{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}) fails for λ=(5,5,5,5,5)\lambda=(5,5,5,5,5).

3. Variations and generalizations

3.1. Relation to ss-Eulerian polynomials

Savage and Visontai introduced the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomials En(𝐬)​(x)E_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})}(x) in [SV15] as the ascent-generating polynomial of 𝐬\mathbf{s}-inversion sequences. Among the various properties uncovered, they showed that this family of polynomials is real-rooted using a similar technique as in Section 2.

Given that the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian and rook-Eulerian polynomials are both real-rooted and satisfy similar-looking recurrences [SV15, Lemma 2.3], it is natural to ask if there is equality between these families of polynomials. We show that rook-Eulerian polynomials are not included in the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomials. Thus, the polynomials QλQ^{\lambda} are a new generalization of the Eulerian polynomials.

Definition 14.

For a sequence 𝐬=(s1,…,sn)\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) of positive integers, the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-inversion sequences are defined by:

ℐn𝐬≔{(e1,…,en)∈ℤn:0≤ei<si​ for ​1≤i≤n}.\mathcal{I}_{n}^{\mathbf{s}}\coloneqq\{(e_{1},\dots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:0\leq e_{i}<s_{i}\text{ for }1\leq i\leq n\}.

The ascent set of an 𝐬\mathbf{s}-inversion sequence 𝐞=(e1,…,en)∈ℐn(𝐬)\mathbf{e}=(e_{1},\dots,e_{n})\in\mathcal{I}_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})} is the set

Asc⁡(𝐞)≔{i∈{0,1,…,n−1}:eisi<ei+1si+1}\Asc(\mathbf{e})\coloneqq\left\{i\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}:\frac{e_{i}}{s_{i}}<\frac{e_{i+1}}{s_{i+1}}\right\}

with the convention that e0=0e_{0}=0 and s0=1s_{0}=1.

The ascent statistic on 𝐞∈ℐn(𝐬)\mathbf{e}\in\mathcal{I}_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})} is defined as:

asc⁡(𝐞)=|Asc⁡(𝐞)|.\asc(\mathbf{e})=|\Asc(\mathbf{e})|.
Definition 15.

Given a sequence 𝐬=(s1,…,sn)\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) of positive integers, the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomial is defined as:

En(𝐬)​(t)=∑𝐞∈ℐn(𝐬)tasc⁡(𝐞).E_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})}(t)=\sum_{\mathbf{e}\in\mathcal{I}_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})}}t^{\asc(\mathbf{e})}.
Example 16.

When 𝐬=(1,2,…,n)\mathbf{s}=(1,2,\ldots,n), by a well-known bijection from inversion sequences to permutations, we get the nthn^{\text{th}} Eulerian polynomial:

En(𝐬)​(t)=An​(t).E_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})}(t)=A_{n}(t).

The following result shows that the family of rook-Eulerian polynomials is distinct from the family of the 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomials.

Theorem 17.

Let λ=(2,3,5,5,5)\lambda=(2,3,5,5,5), there is no sequence 𝐬\mathbf{s} and integer mm such that Qλ=Em(𝐬)Q^{\lambda}=E_{m}^{(\mathbf{s})}.

Proof.

If to the contrary there exists mm and 𝐬\mathbf{s} such that Qλ​(t)=Em(𝐬)​(t)Q^{\lambda}(t)=E_{m}^{(\mathbf{s})}(t), then evaluating both polynomials at t=1t=1 yields ∏i=1msi=∏i=1n(λi−n+i)\prod_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\lambda_{i}-n+i). First note that deleting consecutive 11s in 𝐬\mathbf{s} yields the same 𝐬\mathbf{s}-Eulerian polynomial. This is because if si=si+1=1s_{i}=s_{i+1}=1 for some 0<i<m0<i<m, then each 𝐞∈ℐn(𝐬)\mathbf{e}\in\mathcal{I}_{n}^{(\mathbf{s})} satisfies ei=ei+1=0e_{i}=e_{i+1}=0. In particular, i∉Asc​(𝐞)i\notin\text{Asc}(\mathbf{e}). If we delete the consecutive 11s from 𝐬\mathbf{s} and denote the resulting sequence by 𝐬′\mathbf{s}^{\prime}, we have Em(𝐬)=Em−1(𝐬′).E_{m}^{(\mathbf{s})}=E_{m-1}^{(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})}.

This naturally places an upper bound on the possible values of mm and hence allows us to restrict ourselves to testing finitely many 𝐬\mathbf{s} sequences as possible candidates for the required equality. By exhaustive computer search, there exists no 𝐬\mathbf{s} satisfying ∏i=1msi=∏i=1n(λi−n+i)\prod_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(\lambda_{i}-n+i) for λ=(2,3,5,5,5)\lambda=(2,3,5,5,5). The corresponding QλQ^{\lambda} is equal to

Qλ​(t)=t3+9​t2+13​t+1.Q^{\lambda}(t)=t^{3}+9t^{2}+13t+1.

∎

3.2. Descents in general Bruhat intervals

Given the correspondence between complete rook placements and lower intervals of 312312-avoiding permutations in the Bruhat order, it is natural to ask if the real-rootedness holds for all lower intervals in the Bruhat order. That is, given π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, is

Qπ​(t)=∑σ∈[id,π]Btdes⁡(π)Q^{\pi}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in[\id,\pi]_{B}}t^{\des(\pi)}

real-rooted? As the example below shows, the answer is no, thus highlighting the special nature of the 312312-avoiding condition.

Example 18.

For π=[4,6,2,1,7,3,5]\pi=[4,6,2,1,7,3,5], using 𝙼𝚊𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚖𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚌𝚊\mathtt{Mathematica} one can compute the polynomial QπQ^{\pi} to be

(6) Qπ​(t)=1+43​t+196​t2+168​t3+23​t4+t5,Q^{\pi}(t)=1+43t+196t^{2}+168t^{3}+23t^{4}+t^{5},

which has a pair of non-real roots near −10.8143561±4.5913096​i-10.8143561\pm 4.5913096i. For all permutations in 𝔖6\mathfrak{S}_{6}, we do get real-rooted polynomials by an exhaustive computer search. Note that, as expected, [𝟒,6,𝟐,1,7,𝟑,5][\mathbf{4},6,\mathbf{2},1,7,\mathbf{3},5] contains the pattern 312312.

We can ask the same question for descent-generating polynomials of lower intervals [id,σ]W[\id,\sigma]_{W}; this polynomial also fails to be real-rooted in general, but this time the counterexample has an interesting structure.

Recall that given a poset PP on nn elements, the Jordan–Hölder set ℒ⁡(P)\mathcal{L}(P) of PP, is the set of inverses of linear extensions of PP, and WPW_{P} is the descent-generating polynomial of ℒ⁡(P)\mathcal{L}(P):

ℒ⁡(P)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(P) ={σ∈𝔖n:i⪯Pj⟹σi−1<σj−1},\displaystyle=\{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}:i\preceq_{P}j\implies\sigma_{i}^{-1}<\sigma_{j}^{-1}\},
WP\displaystyle W_{P} =∑σ∈ℒ⁡(𝒫)tdes⁡(σ).\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{L(P)}}t^{\des(\sigma)}.

Permutations naturally give rise to the following class of posets.

Definition 19.

Let σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. The partial order in the permutation poset Pσ=([n],⪯)P_{\sigma}=([n],\preceq) is defined as

i⪯j⇔i≤jandσi≤σj.i\preceq j\quad\iff\quad i\leq j\;\text{and}\;\sigma_{i}\leq\sigma_{j}.

The following lemma can be seen by interpreting the cover relation in the weak order in terms of containment of inversion sets.

Lemma 20.

[FW97, Lemma 5] The Jordan–Hölder set of PσP_{\sigma} equals the lower interval [id,σ]W[\id,\sigma]_{W} in the weak order on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}.

Recall that the width of a poset is the size of the largest antichain of the poset. The following lemma is well-known.

Lemma 21.

[CP23, Section 11.5][FW97, pg. 5] Every naturally labeled poset PP of width two is a permutation poset.

By combining the previous two lemmata, we have the folowing.

Proposition 22.

Let QWπ​(t)=∑σ∈[id,π]Wtdes⁡(π)Q^{\pi}_{W}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in[\id,\pi]_{W}}t^{\des(\pi)}. There exists π∈𝔖17\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{17} such that QWπ​(t)Q^{\pi}_{W}(t) is not real-rooted.

Proof.

From Lemma 20, we have the following equality of polynomials: QWπ=WP⁡(π)Q^{\pi}_{W}=W_{P(\pi)}. Now, there exists a naturally labeled poset PP of width two such that WPW_{P} is not real-rooted [Ste07]. By Lemma 21, it follows that there exists π\pi such that P=PπP=P_{\pi}. It follows that QWπQ^{\pi}_{W} is not real-rooted. Concretely, let π∈𝔖17\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{17} be defined by

π=[2,4,6,8,10,1,12,3,15,5,17,7,9,11,13,14,16].\pi=[2,4,6,8,10,1,12,3,15,5,17,7,9,11,13,14,16].

Then, using 𝙼𝚊𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚖𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚌𝚊\mathtt{Mathematica}, the polynomial QWπ​(t)=∑σ∈[id,π]Wtdes⁡(π)Q^{\pi}_{W}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in[\id,\pi]_{W}}t^{\des(\pi)} is equal to

(7) 3​t8+86​t7+658​t6+1946​t5+2534​t4+1420​t3+336​t2+32​t+1,3t^{8}+86t^{7}+658t^{6}+1946t^{5}+2534t^{4}+1420t^{3}+336t^{2}+32t+1,

which has a pair of non-real roots at −1.85884±0.14976​i-1.85884\pm 0.14976i. ∎

In [AJ24], the so-called poset – skew shape correspondence was used to prove that WPW_{P} is ultra-log-concave for naturally labeled width two posets PP. This together with Lemma 21 and Proposition 22 makes the class of general permutation posets a good candidate for further investigation in this vein.

Conjecture 23.

Let π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Then QWπQ_{W}^{\pi} is ultra-log-concave.

Note that this is a special case of Brenti’s conjecture [Bre89, Conjecture 1.1] rephrased in the language of the weak order.

For width two posets, the PP-Eulerian polynomial is closely related to the peak-generating polynomial of ℒ⁡(P)\mathcal{L}(P) (see [Ste07, Proposition 1.1]). Based on this relation, we can modify π\pi in (7) and obtain

π~=[3,5,7,9,11,2,13,4,16,6,18,8,10,12,14,15,17,18],\widetilde{\pi}=[3,5,7,9,11,2,13,4,16,6,18,8,10,12,14,15,17,18],

such that the peak-generating polynomial

∑σ≤Wπ~tpeak⁡(σ)\sum_{\sigma\leq_{W}\widetilde{\pi}}t^{\peak(\sigma)}

is also equal to (7), and hence not real-rooted.

Recall that an excedance of a permutation σ\sigma, is an instance ii where σi>i\sigma_{i}>i. The number of excedances of a permutation is denoted exc⁡(σ)\exc(\sigma). It is well-known that the classical Eulerian polynomials can also be defined via the excedance statistic: An​(t)=∑σ∈𝔖ntexc⁡(σ)A_{n}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\exc(\sigma)}. It is therefore natural to ask if excedances also gives rise to real-rooted polynomials when considering intervals in the Bruhat order. Computer experiments suggests the following conjecture.

Conjecture 24.

Let π\pi be 312-avoiding. Then

(8) ∑σ≤Bπtexc⁡(σ)\sum_{\sigma\leq_{B}\pi}t^{\exc(\sigma)}

is real-rooted.

Again, we cannot extend this conjecture to general π\pi, as the polynomial

(9) ∑σ≤B[4,1,5,6,8,2,3,7]texc⁡(σ)=1+21t+140t2+290t3+127t4+5t5\sum_{\sigma\leq_{B}[4,1,5,6,8,2,3,7]}t^{\exc(\sigma)}=1+21t+140t^{2}+290t^{3}+127t^{4}+5t^{5}

has some non-real roots.

3.3. Multiset rook-Eulerian polynomials

We now consider the setting of rook placements on boards wherein each row contains exactly one rook, but a single column can now contain more than one rook. The context for this set-up is Simion’s multiset Eulerian polynomials [Sim84], which were also shown to be real-rooted. These polynomials have since been refined and generalized in various directions; see [MP23] for instance. We offer a generalization that considers arbitrary Ferrers boards.

Let α=(α1,…,αk)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dotsc,\alpha_{k}) be non-negative integers with total sum nn, and let λ\lambda and μ\mu be integer partitions such that λi>μi\lambda_{i}>\mu_{i} for all ii. We let 𝒲⁡(λ/μ,α)\mathcal{W}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha) be all words with αi\alpha_{i} entries equal to ii, such that

μi<wi≤λi for all i=1,2,…,n.\mu_{i}<w_{i}\leq\lambda_{i}\quad\text{ for all $i=1,2,\dotsc,n$}.

The vector α\alpha is the content of each of the words in 𝒲⁡(λ/μ,α)\mathcal{W}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha). The partitions λ/μ\lambda/\mu are usually called a skew Ferrers board.

Example 25.

Consider all words with content α=(2,2,1)\alpha=(2,2,1) and the Ferrers board λ=22233\lambda=22233. There are in total 30 words with the given content (permutations of 1122311223), but only 1212 of these fit on the board λ\lambda:

Let α\alpha be a non-negative integer vector with total sum nn. The multiset rook-Eulerian polynomial R⁡(λ/μ,α,t)R(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t) is defined as

(10) R⁡(λ/μ,α,t)≔∑w∈𝒲⁡(λ/μ,α)tasc⁡(w).R(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t)\coloneqq\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha)}t^{\asc(w)}.
Example 26.

The board λ=22233\lambda=22233 and α=(2,2,1)\alpha=(2,2,1) as in Example 25 gives

R⁡(λ/μ,α,t)=t3+8​t2+3​t.R(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t)=t^{3}+8t^{2}+3t.

As before, we introduce a refined version of the ascent-generating polynomials, based on the first entry of the words:

(11) Rj​(λ/μ,α,t)≔∑w∈𝒲⁡(λ/μ,α)w1=jtasc⁡(w).R_{j}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t)\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha)\\ w_{1}=j\end{subarray}}t^{\asc(w)}.

It follows immediately that

(12) R⁡(λ/μ,α,t)=∑jRj​(λ/μ,α,t).R(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t)=\sum_{j}R_{j}(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t).

The refined multiset Eulerian polynomials satisfy the recursion below. Note that in this case, we do not insert an extra column in the diagram as in Lemma 10. We only prepend an additional first row.

Lemma 27.

Let λ=(λ1,…,λn)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{n}) and let λ+=(m,λ1,…,λn)\lambda^{+}=(m,\lambda_{1},\dotsc,\lambda_{n}) where m≤λ1m\leq\lambda_{1}. Suppose i≤mi\leq m and let α+=α+𝐞i\alpha^{+}=\alpha+\mathbf{e}_{i}. Then we have the recursion

(13) Ri​(λ+,α+,t)=∑j=1iRj​(λ,α,t)+t​∑j=i+1λ1Rj​(λ,α,t).R_{i}(\lambda^{+},\alpha^{+};t)=\sum_{j=1}^{i}R_{j}(\lambda,\alpha;t)+t\sum_{j=i+1}^{\lambda_{1}}R_{j}(\lambda,\alpha;t).
Proof.

This is the same argument as in Lemma 10. ∎

The following conjecture generalizes a result by Simion [Sim84, Sect. 2].

Conjecture 28.

For Ferrers boards, the polynomial R⁡(λ,α,t)R(\lambda,\alpha;t) is real-rooted. Moreover,

(14) Rλ1​(λ,α,t),Rλ1−1​(λ,α,t),…,R2​(λ,α,t),R1​(λ,α,t)R_{\lambda_{1}}(\lambda,\alpha;t),R_{\lambda_{1}-1}(\lambda,\alpha;t),\dotsc,R_{2}(\lambda,\alpha;t),R_{1}(\lambda,\alpha;t)

forms an interlacing sequence.

In the case when λ\lambda is a rectangular Ferrers board, a result of Simion asserts that R⁡(λ,α,t)R(\lambda,\alpha;t) is real-rooted for any fixed α\alpha [Sim84]. The interlacing property in the rectangle case is covered by the more recent paper by Ma and Pan [MP23, Theorem 1.11]. See also [BHVW11, Eq. (4.7)] for a stable multivariate generalization of Simion’s result.

Remark 29.

We cannot hope to obtain real-rootedness when extending the multiset setting to skew shapes. For the board λ/μ=333321/11\lambda/\mu=333321/11 and content α=(2,2,2)\alpha=(2,2,2), we find that R⁡(λ/μ,α,t)=t4+4​t3+6​t2+tR(\lambda/\mu,\alpha;t)=t^{4}+4t^{3}+6t^{2}+t, which has some non-real roots.
